growth_story.headline: Denmark's income per person is at its highest yet after decades of steady, modest growth, but recent gains rest heavily on the drug industry.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Denmark's income per person has grown at a steady, modest pace, averaging 1.3 percent a year over 1990–2025, with no lasting shift in that trend. The weakest stretch was 2006–2015, when growth averaged 0.2 percent a year: a housing boom that peaked in 2007 ended in large price falls, income per person fell 5.5 percent in 2009, and the IMF called the recovery anemic as households paid down high debts slowly. Income per person did not pass its 2007 level until 2016. Growth then picked up to 1.6 percent a year over 2016–2025, despite a fall of 2.1 percent in 2020 and a rebound of 6.0 percent in 2021. Since 2022 the IMF and the OECD describe an economy running at two speeds, with pharmaceutical exports driving output while the rest of the economy grew slowly, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.text: Recent growth has come mostly from pharmaceutical exports, while spending at home stayed weak. Outside the drug industry, output shrank in 2022 and 2023 and recovered only slowly after that.

The IMF expects US tariffs to hit Denmark only lightly, because goods made in Denmark that pass through customs are a small share of its exports, but wider trade tensions cloud the outlook for a small, open economy.

since_last_year.text: In mid-2025 the IMF expected growth to slow as the pharmaceutical boom began to normalize. By September 2026 it expected growth to strengthen in 2026, still led by drug exports, while the rest of the economy grew at a more moderate pace. Income per person rose 2.4 percent in 2025 and reached a new high.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes strong growth since 2022, but income per person dipped in 2022 (-0.3 percent) and 2023 (-0.1 percent) before rising in 2024 and 2025. The OECD's finding that output outside the drug industry shrank in those two years sits closer to what income per person shows. The IMF also described growth after the global financial crisis as markedly slower than before it, yet the data's era test finds no lasting shift in growth since 1990, only a weak decade averaging 0.2 percent a year over 2006–2015.
